name: Babes in Toyland
label: Twin/Tone
lede: A drummer who had never played, a guitarist who told Soul Asylum's singer she'd beat his band before she had one, and a John Peel obsession that turned a Twin/Tone album into a UK indie number one.

eras.title: My band is going to kick your band's ass
eras.text: Kat Bjelland leaves a short-lived Portland and San Francisco project behind, moves to Minneapolis, and finds a drummer who has never played drums. They build a following in galleries and basements and put out one single.

years.src: Wikipedia: Pagan Babies (band) · Wikipedia: Kat Bjelland · Dangerous Minds: Sugar Baby Doll
years.h: Kat Bjelland and Courtney Love start a band called Sugar Babydoll
years.p: Bjelland says she met Love at a Portland nightclub in 1984. The band moved to San Francisco, cut a four-track demo in December 1985, and was gone by 1986.
years.xp:
Wikipedia gives the group several names: Sugar Babydoll, Sugar Babylon, Sugar Bunny Farm, then Pagan Babies, with Jennifer Finch, later of L7, on bass. Love has described the sound as faux Cocteau Twins. Bjelland began writing heavier songs, Love objected to what she called "that punk rock noise," and Love left.

Bjelland's own summary: "We went through a few names, and we only played a couple of shows." Two of the songs lived on. "Quiet Room" was re-recorded by Babes in Toyland for the To Mother EP and again for Fontanelle, and "Best Sunday Dress" reappeared on Hole's 1998 single "Celebrity Skin".

years.src: Wikipedia: Babes in Toyland (band) · Wikipedia: Lori Barbero · The Current: Kat Bjelland on Babes in Toyland and her long and winding career · MinnPost: From a Minneapolis art gallery's basement to the heights of the alternative rock scene: Babes in Toyland
years.h: A barbecue in Minneapolis: Lori Barbero has never played drums
years.p: [[Kat Bjelland|46f4f238-6edc-4e59-87bf-523a508bdc57]] had moved from San Francisco to start a band, and she asked Barbero to be its drummer on the spot. Kris Holetz and Cindy Russell filled out the first line-up.
years.xp:
Barbero, born in Minneapolis and raised partly in Pearl River, New York, had spent teenage trips at CBGB but had no instrument experience. That was the plan. Bjelland told The Current in 2013: "I wanted musicians who didn't know how to play very well so then you could create a sound together."

Russell and Holetz were gone quickly and Michelle Leon took the bass. The first shows were in a Minneapolis art gallery basement, then the Cabooze and the 7th Street Entry. Sources spell the first bassist's name Kris or Chris Holetz.

years.cap: Babes in Toyland performing in Minneapolis at Cedarfest, August, 1995 · Wikimedia
years.src: The Current: Kat Bjelland on Babes in Toyland and her long and winding career · The Current: Behind First Avenue's Stars: Babes in Toyland
years.h: Bjelland tells Dave Pirner her band will kick his band's ass
years.p: She said it to the Soul Asylum singer at First Avenue, about five months after arriving in town. The band did not exist yet.
years.xp:
Bjelland tells it in The Current's 2013 interview: she had come from San Francisco because Minneapolis, with Soul Asylum and the Replacements, felt tight-knit, and she walked up to [[Dave Pirner|8849e71c-181b-444b-8cfb-09445e6231d4]] with the line "My band is gonna kick your band's ass." She then had to build the band.

The Current's First Avenue feature counts 33 shows at First Avenue and the 7th Street Entry between 1988 and 2000.

years.src: Wikipedia: Babes in Toyland (band) · John Peel Wiki: Babes In Toyland
years.h: Dust Cake Boy 7" on Treehouse Records
years.p: The first record: a single with "Spit to See the Shine" on the flip, recorded in Seattle in October 1988.
years.xp: Wikipedia lists a 1989 release for the black 7" on Treehouse, recorded at Technisound in Seattle in October 1988 (the band's page dates the single 1988). It was the record that reached [[John Peel|e4dec348-ad10-43b6-a2b1-c22aab890675]]: the BBC DJ played the single on air in 1989, before any album existed.

eras.title: Twin/Tone's oddest band
eras.text: An album cut in Seattle, a tour with Sonic Youth and a DJ in England who cannot stop playing them. Twin/Tone, the Minneapolis label of the Replacements and Soul Asylum, has a band it does not quite know what to do with.

years.src: Twin/Tone: Babes in Toyland · Wikipedia: Spanking Machine · Sonic Archives: A Conversation with Kat Bjelland of Babes In Toyland
yt: "He's My Thing" video, shot at First Avenue
years.h: Spanking Machine: recorded by [[Jack Endino|d06cca33-9167-4049-b5ce-6a6aeff60a8d]] in Seattle
years.p: Eleven songs on Twin/Tone (TTR 89183), cut at Reciprocal Recording, the studio Nirvana and Mudhoney used.
years.xp:
Twin/Tone lists the release as April 16, 1990. Jack Endino produced and engineered it; "Dust Cake Boy" came over from the Treehouse single. Rolling Stone later put it at number 27 on a list of the 50 greatest grunge albums.

In a January 1990 interview in Minneapolis's The New Puritan ReView, done over pitchers at the Black Forest Inn, Bjelland said of the label: "We're really this odd fucking band to be on Twin/Tone. We don't really sound like what they have." She later called it the band's first real press.

years.cap: Babes in Toyland and Sonic Youth
years.src: Sonic Archives: A Conversation with Kat Bjelland of Babes In Toyland · Wikipedia: Spanking Machine · Wikipedia: Babes in Toyland (band)
years.h: Sonic Youth watches Babes at the 7th Street Entry, then takes them to Europe
years.p: [[Thurston Moore|8ba48525-d922-42ee-9775-97b7b8f9712e]] invited the band on Sonic Youth's 1990 European tour after seeing them play, and Sonic Youth brought them back to Reading in 1991.
years.xp:
Bjelland has described Sonic Youth walking over to the 7th Street Entry after their own First Avenue set to catch Babes in Toyland. It started what she called a fruitful relationship between the two bands.

Most of the band's early fan mail came from England and Spain, she said.

q: If either of my daughters was in a band like that, I'd be well proud of it.
years.src: John Peel Wiki: Babes In Toyland · Wikipedia: Babes in Toyland (band)
years.h: John Peel: "If either of my daughters was in a band like that..."
years.p: Peel called a gig above a pub in Bedford one of his favorite concerts and named Spanking Machine his album of 1990.
years.xp: Peel's wiki lists five BBC sessions with the band between 1990 and 1995. He announced Spanking Machine as his favourite album of 1990 on December 22. "Bruise Violet" reached number 9 in his 1992 Festive Fifty. Two of the early sessions were compiled as the Peel Sessions EP (Strange Fruit, 1992).

years.src: Wikipedia: To Mother (EP) · Twin/Tone: Babes in Toyland
years.h: To Mother sits at number one on the UK indie chart for ten weeks
years.p: Seven songs recorded at Southern Studios in London with John Loder. The cover is a childhood photo of Bjelland's mother.
years.xp:
Bjelland's mother died of pancreatic cancer while the EP was being made, and her photo became the cover and the title's source, according to Wikipedia. The chart run: number one on the UK Indie Chart for ten of its thirteen weeks.

Release date is disputed: Twin/Tone's own page says June 14, Wikipedia says July 1. Reviews split. NME gave it 8 out of 10, Robert Christgau gave it his lowest grade. Twin/Tone's records show 7,388 units sold before the band left for Reprise.

years.src: Wikipedia: Babes in Toyland (band) · First Avenue: Babes in Toyland
yt: Babes in Toyland, The Year Punk Broke, 1991
years.h: Reading Festival, and the film that caught it: 1991: The Year Punk Broke
years.p: Babes in Toyland played with Sonic Youth on the European run that [[Dave Markey|c48f5a63-0b7c-4bbc-b8bb-64474ad7c77c]] filmed, including Reading.
years.xp: First Avenue's page says the band played Reading three times: 1991, 1993 and 1995. The 1991 set is in Markey's tour documentary alongside Sonic Youth, Nirvana and Dinosaur Jr.

years.src: Wikipedia: Babes in Toyland (band) · Wikipedia: Michelle Leon · Wikipedia: Kinderwhore
years.h: Courtney Love and the bass chair: three accounts
years.p: Bjelland and Barbero say that is what they told Love when she picked up an instrument at their rehearsal. Love says she was kicked out. Leon says Love briefly replaced her.
years.xp:
On the record: Bjelland and Love had been in Sugar Babydoll and Pagan Babies together, and Love lived in Bjelland's house at some point. In a 2015 interview Bjelland and Barbero said: "She lived in my house, and one time I think when we were rehearsing she came down and probably picked up something and tried to play." That is when they said, "get out of here."

Love has said she was kicked out. Michelle Leon, in her memoir I Live Inside (Minnesota Historical Society Press, 2016), says Love briefly replaced her after a couple of rehearsals, and Barbero then phoned to ask Leon back. The accounts differ, and this page does not pick one.

eras.title: A purple 7-inch and a major label
eras.text: A Warner Bros. A&R man with a Minneapolis history gets the band onto Reprise. A new bassist, a Sonic Youth producer, Cindy Sherman's loft and a tour bill with Primus and Rage Against the Machine.

years.src: Wikipedia: Michelle Leon · Wikipedia: Maureen Herman · Wikipedia: Bruise Violet
years.h: Michelle Leon leaves. Maureen Herman takes over on bass
years.p: Leon left in early 1992, after the murder of her boyfriend Joe Cole, according to Wikipedia. Herman, a Libertyville, Illinois native, joined for Fontanelle.
years.xp: Herman had learned bass in 1988 and had a band called M&M Stigmata. At Libertyville High School she worked on the student paper with Tom Morello and Adam Jones, both of whom she would later share a bill with. Leon is listed on the "Bruise Violet" recording made in February 1992; Herman is on the album released that August.

years.src: The Current: Musicheads Essential Artist: Babes in Toyland · The Current: Kat Bjelland on Babes in Toyland and her long and winding career
years.h: Tim Carr takes the band to Reprise
years.p: The Minneapolis critic turned Warner Bros. A&R man championed them, and the band signed to Reprise.
years.xp: Bjelland has said that Carr did not try to change the band's sound, and that they signed before the Nirvana rush. The Current's profile credits Carr with taking them to Reprise.

years.src: Wikipedia: Fontanelle (album) · Wikipedia: Babes in Toyland (band) · The Current: Musicheads Essential Artist: Babes in Toyland
years.h: Fontanelle: Lee Ranaldo produces, Cindy Sherman shoots the cover
years.p: Cindy Sherman shot the cover: a nude doll before a mirror. Reprise released it August 11, 1992.
years.xp: Recorded at Pachyderm Studio in Cannon Falls, Minnesota and Sorcerer Sound in New York. Ranaldo produced with Bjelland, Brian Paulson engineered and Dave Ogilvie mixed. It reached number 24 on the UK Albums Chart. The Current puts US sales at about 220,000; Wikipedia's band page says 250,000.

years.src: Wikipedia: Bruise Violet · Wikipedia: Fontanelle (album)
years.h: "Bruise Violet": ten women from a Brooklyn motorcycle gang in blonde wigs
years.p: Gretchen Bender shot it in Minneapolis, at CBGB and on the Brooklyn Bridge. Sherman appears as Bjelland's double.
years.xp:
The extras wore blonde wigs and babydoll dresses to match Bjelland. The video debuted on MTV's 120 Minutes in October 1992 and turned up on Beavis and Butt-Head in the episode "Babes-R-Us." The single came out in November on purple 7" vinyl with "Magic Flute" and "Gone."

Some listeners read the song as a swipe at Courtney Love. Bjelland has denied that and said Violet was a shared muse.

years.src: Wikipedia: Painkillers (EP) · Wikipedia: Babes in Toyland (band)
years.h: Painkillers lands during Lollapalooza
years.p: An EP of outtakes from the Fontanelle sessions, recorded at Pachyderm and CBGB and put out on Reprise (Southern in the UK).
years.xp: Wikipedia dates it June 22, 1993. Producers across the tracks: [[Jack Endino|d06cca33-9167-4049-b5ce-6a6aeff60a8d]], Bjelland, [[Lee Ranaldo|6eb1f3f8-5c5a-41c2-a390-f397a2b824a3]] and Barbero. It charted at number 53 on the UK Albums Chart.

years.src: Wikipedia: Babes in Toyland (band) · The Current: Behind First Avenue's Stars: Babes in Toyland · Rolling Stone: Babes in Toyland Return as Ferocious as Ever at L.A. Comeback Show · Wikipedia: Maureen Herman
years.h: Lollapalooza 1993: Primus, Alice in Chains, Rage Against the Machine
years.p: Herman's high school newspaper classmates [[Tom Morello|42a636a0-dbe4-4d0c-abe2-1590fad9531b]] and [[Adam Jones|82856c21-c448-4432-bc79-97009b7eb853]] were on the same bill.
years.xp: Also on the tour: Dinosaur Jr. and Tool. Barbero told The Current a FedEx package with a peanut butter and jelly sandwich reached her during a sold-out show, a gift from Jones. Morello, introducing the band at the Roxy in 2015, said they had inspired him since Lollapalooza 1993.

years.src: Wikipedia: Babes in Toyland (band) · Wikipedia: Kat Bjelland
years.h: A benefit show in Miami on the day Kurt Cobain is found
years.p: Babes in Toyland played the Cameo Theatre for Rock Against Domestic Violence with 7 Year Bitch and Jack Off Jill.
years.xp: Wikipedia describes the show as the same day Nirvana's Kurt Cobain was found dead in his Seattle home. Wikipedia's article on Bjelland says she had a nervous breakdown after Cobain's death and notes a period of heroin addiction in the 1990s.

years.src: Wikipedia: Live Through This · Wikipedia: Kat Bjelland
years.h: Bjelland co-writes "I Think That I Would Die" on Hole's Live Through This
years.p: It is the only song on the album with a credited writer beyond Courtney Love and Eric Erlandson.
years.xp: The liner notes credit Love, Erlandson and Bjelland. Bjelland also had a band called Crunt from 1993 to 1995 with her then-husband Stuart Gray.

eras.title: The label, the bassist, the last tour
eras.text: A third album that the press found softer, a bass chair that keeps changing and a record deal that does not survive. The band winds down in fits, then plays a last tour.

years.src: Wikipedia: Nemesisters
years.h: Nemesisters: recorded live in the room at AmRep Studios
years.p: The band cut it together with producer Tim Mac in Minneapolis and covered Sister Sledge's "We Are Family."
years.xp: "Sweet '69" reached number 37 on Modern Rock Tracks and "We Are Family" number 22 on Hot Dance Music/Club Play. Reviews were mixed. Stephen Thomas Erlewine wrote at AllMusic that most of the raw, slashing guitars were gone, replaced by a "pulsing, plodding grind." Spin's Lorraine Ali said the album lacked the conviction and direction of its predecessors.

years.src: Wikipedia: Maureen Herman · Wikipedia: Babes in Toyland (band) · First Avenue: Babes in Toyland
years.h: Maureen Herman quits, and Reprise drops the band
years.p: Herman cited hip problems and frustration with the industry. Dana Cochrane, formerly of Mickey Finn, played bass live in 1996 and 1997.
years.xp: Herman said of the period: "I couldn't remember the last time I had enjoyed music either as a player or a listener." Wikipedia says Michelle Leon briefly rejoined in 1997 and that the band moved between breakups and reformations. First Avenue's page gives Herman's departure as 1997.

years.src: Wikipedia: Kat Bjelland · The Current: Kat Bjelland on Babes in Toyland and her long and winding career
years.h: Bjelland forms Katastrophy Wife with drummer Glen Mattson
years.p: The band released Amusia in 2001 and All Kneel in 2004.
years.xp: Bjelland stepped back from performing between about 2002 and 2005, she told The Current. Wikipedia notes she publicly discussed a schizoaffective disorder diagnosis in 2007.

years.src: Wikipedia: Babes in Toyland (band) · The Current: Behind First Avenue's Stars: Babes in Toyland · First Avenue: Babes in Toyland
years.h: The last tour ends in Minneapolis: Minneapolism
years.p: Bjelland, Barbero and new bassist Jessie Farmer play a hometown show, recorded and released as Minneapolism.
years.xp: Wikipedia dates the band's end to 2001; First Avenue's page says the final show was November 25, 2000 and lists Bjelland and Barbero. In 2002 Bjelland played shows in Europe as Babes in Toyland with the British band Angelica and stopped using the name after Barbero and Herman raised legal issues.

eras.title: The reunion nobody expected
eras.text: Bjelland says she swore off a reunion. Fans, a phone call and a tour later, they play sold-out rooms for two years, and then it ends again.

years.src: Wikipedia: Babes in Toyland (band) · WXPN: Babes in Toyland Rides Again
years.h: Bjelland and Herman confirm the reunion on Lancer Radio
years.p: The talk was on a Pasadena College radio station. Herman had passed along an offer of money from fans.
years.xp: According to WXPN, wealthy fans offered to finance a comeback, and Herman kept contacting Bjelland until she agreed to consider it. Barbero told the station: "I didn't realize how void and empty I was not playing music and not being with Kat."

q: I said I'd never, ever do a reunion.
years.src: Rolling Stone: Babes in Toyland Return as Ferocious as Ever at L.A. Comeback Show · Wikipedia: Babes in Toyland (band)
years.h: The Roxy, Los Angeles: Tom Morello introduces them
years.p: A warm-up show at Pappy and Harriet's in Pioneertown on February 10, then the Roxy: 45 minutes, 13 songs.
years.xp: Morello called them "the princesses of punk, the matriarchs of metal and the goddesses of grunge." Guests in the crowd included Patty Schemel, Eric Erlandson, Brody Dalle, Exene Cervenka and members of the Melvins and the Jesus Lizard. Bjelland told Rolling Stone she changed her mind because she got older and wanted her 15-year-old son to see the band.

years.src: Wikipedia: Babes in Toyland (band) · WXPN: Babes in Toyland Rides Again
yt: "Bruise Violet" live at Rock the Garden
years.h: Rock the Garden at the Walker Art Center, Minneapolis
years.p: A two-day festival on the museum's lawn, the hometown return with Herman on bass.
years.xp: The tour that summer took them across England, Scotland, Spain, Italy, Bumbershoot in Seattle and the Montreal Pop Festival. The set leaned on old songs rather than new ones, WXPN reported, and the fall dates started at Underground Arts in Philadelphia.

years.src: Wikipedia: Babes in Toyland (band) · Wikipedia: Maureen Herman · WXPN: Babes in Toyland Rides Again
years.h: Herman is fired mid-tour; Clara Salyer takes over
years.p: Barbero said the decision made her and Bjelland sick with stress. Herman, months later, said it followed an essay she wrote for Boing Boing.
years.xp:
Barbero's statement: "Two months before we let her go, Kat and I were so upset we couldn't eat, we couldn't sleep." Herman said in December 2015 that the firing followed her Boing Boing piece about Jackie Fox of the Runaways and her assault allegation against manager Kim Fowley, which conflicted with Barbero's business ties to Joan Jett's Blackheart Records.

Salyer stayed on bass until 2017.

years.src: Wikipedia: Babes in Toyland (band) · First Avenue: Babes in Toyland · The Current: Behind First Avenue's Stars: Babes in Toyland
years.h: The band plays its last shows
years.p: Wikipedia says they disbanded after 2017, and Bjelland stopped performing; First Avenue lists a September 22, 2017 show as the most recent.
years.xp: In May 2020, Barbero said on Conan Neutron's Protonic Reversal podcast that there was very little chance of future reunions. The band also has a star on the outside mural at First Avenue, honoring artists who have sold out the club or shaped it. Selena Chambers wrote the 33 1/3 book on Fontanelle, published by Bloomsbury in 2023.
